Chart system 01 · Explainer · Stretch test

Six new forms

Six forms the ten Explainer charts lack, from the range of Dustin’s newspaper references: shift arrows, a tile map of shifts, small-multiple sparklines, monthly columns with an average, a results table and a bubble map. Each is drawn by a generator on Explainer’s kit, on Newsprint, from the shared chart data.

Three of the six show election results. Party marks stay in neutral inks with the party named in words, and arrows and position carry direction. No chart on this page takes the working red, and only the results table moves: it sorts by any column.

ShowHide how to read our charts, in short
  1. The black label names the kind of evidence. A Finding is something measured; an Estimate depends on stated assumptions.
  2. The title is the answer in one sentence. “Would” or “may” in a title marks a less certain claim.
  3. The gray line under the title says what was counted, in what unit, where and when.
  4. The dark mark is what the title is about; gray marks are there to compare.
  5. Notes in and under the chart explain anything drawn in an unusual way, such as a line that breaks.
  6. The source line says who collected the numbers. Open the table under any chart to see every value.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S11 Shift arrows

Reader question
Which states moved toward which party between 2020 and 2024, and how far?
Why this form
Arrows on one margin axis show where each state stood and how far it moved, and the six arrows that cross the even line show where the leader changed.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S12 Tile-grid map with shift arrows

Reader question
Where did the shift happen?
Why this form
A tile gives every state the same weight, and an arrow inside it puts the size of the shift where the state sits, so a reader finds a region before a number.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S13 Small-multiple sparklines

Reader question
Which sectors added jobs since January 2022, and which lost them?
Why this form
Small panels on one scale let a reader compare fourteen industries at a glance, and the totals sit in their own rows so a whole never reads as one of its parts.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S14 Columns with a moving average

Reader question
How many jobs did the economy add each month?
Why this form
Columns show each month’s change, noise and all, and the three-month average drawn over them gives the trend a reader can repeat.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S15 Results table

Reader question
How did each state vote in 2024, and how did that compare with 2020?
Why this form
A table answers a lookup: a reader finds their state, reads both margins with the leader named, and sorts by any column to find the biggest shifts.

Studio note, not part of the chart

S16 Bubble map

Reader question
Where did eligible voters turn out, and where are most of them?
Why this form
Circles sized by eligible voters show where most of them live, and one ink stepped by turnout shows how many voted, so size and rate read together.

New tokens

The sizes these six forms add to Explainer’s chart tokens, in one dict the kit can adopt. Every other size on this page is an Explainer token.

STRETCH_TOKENS, which extends CHART_TOKENS
TokenValueUsed by
arrow{“shaft”: 2, “head_len”: 8, “head_half”: 4.5, “phone_head_len”: 6, “phone_head_half”: 3.5, “tail_r”: 2.25, “tip_r”: 0.5, “key_points”: 10}S11, S12, S15: arrowheads, tails and the dot at the tip
shift_axis{“pitch”: 20, “phone_pitch”: 19, “label”: 14, “break_gap”: 32, “far_segment”: [−90, −80], “near_segment”: [−40, 50], “tick_step”: 10, “phone_tick_step”: 20}S11: row pitch, label size, the break between the far and near segments
tile{“size_max”: 80, “gap”: 6, “mid_gap”: 4, “phone_gap”: 2.5, “phone_cols”: 11, “frame”: 2}S12: tile size, gaps, the eleven-column phone grid, the frame on a changed state
tile_arrow{“angle_small”: 62, “angle_large”: 22, “phone_angle_small”: 42, “phone_angle_large”: 12, “angle_ref”: 12, “key_points”: [1, 5, 10], “phone_head_len”: 5, “phone_head_half”: 3}S12: arrow angle, steep for a small shift and flat for a large one; the key’s sample shifts
spark{“px_per_point”: 2.5, “phone_px_per_point”: 2.5, “domain”: [−15, 20], “ticks”: [−10, 0, 10, 20], “line”: 2, “context”: 1.5, “end_r”: 3, “row_height”: 42, “gap_x”: 30, “phone_gap_x”: 18}S13: vertical scale shared by every sparkline, domain, line weights, end dot, row height, gutters
columns{“fill_share”: 0.72, “avg_line”: 3, “prelim_months”: 2, “vertex_r”: 1.5, “domain”: [−200, 450]}S14: column width as a share of the month, the average line, preliminary months, the domain
bubble{“r_max”: {“wide”: 50, “mid”: 34, “phone”: 23, “small_phone”: 21}, “gap”: 2, “outline”: 1, “bins”: [60, 65, 70, 75], “key_millions”: [1, 5, 20], “label_pad”: 3}S16: largest circle radius per artboard, the gap between circles, the outline, turnout bins, the size key
results{“row”: 38, “half”: 136, “half_points”: 90, “bar”: 3, “shift_px_per_point”: 6.5, “shift_head”: 6}S15: row height, the half-cell for each margin, the bar under it, the shift arrow scale

On Charcoal

Two of the six on Charcoal. The jobs chart, because charts of monthly numbers travel as dark social cards; the bubble map, because its turnout ramp has to run the other way on a dark ground, lighter for more.

On phones

Every figure at 358 pixels, the width its phone drawing is made for, set side by side so all six read on one screen. These are the same figures as on Newsprint, with the same data and attributes.

Data: Federal Election Commission official results for 2020 and 2024; U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics payroll series via FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis; U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey, November 2024; all retrieved November 6, 2026.
